questions.text: What does runtime.Goexit do in a goroutine?
options: Ends the goroutine after its defers; it is not a panic
The same as return from main

questions.text: Since Go 1.22, what happens to the loop variable in go func(){ ... i }?
options: All goroutines see one i after the loop
Each iteration has its own variable
i is copied only when GOMAXPROCS > 1

questions.text: What does GOMAXPROCS(1) mean for goroutines?
options: At most one Go thread runs at a time; goroutines still interleave

questions.text: Why is a goroutine spinning on for {} that nobody waits for a leak?
options: It occupies a separate OS process
for {} is forbidden by the language
It will not finish on its own and keeps stack and state until process exit

questions.text: What does runtime.Gosched do?
options: Hints the scheduler to yield the CPU to another goroutine

questions.text: Two goroutines write one variable with no synchronization. What is that?
options: A data race: the result is undefined
The compiler inserts a lock by itself
Fine if the type is int

questions.text: How does a goroutine’s stack behave?
options: A fixed 8 MiB, like an OS thread
Starts small and grows as needed (and may shrink)
One stack shared by all goroutines

questions.text: A local whose address is sent to a goroutine, after the creating function returns:
options: The compiler moves it to the heap; the pointer stays valid

questions.text: runtime.Goexit is a panic, so recover catches it.
Defers in a goroutine still run on Goexit.
GOMAXPROCS(1) forbids more than one goroutine.
Since Go 1.22 each for iteration has its own loop variable.
Unsynchronized writes to one variable from two goroutines are a data race.
A goroutine’s stack starts as large as an OS thread stack.
Gosched ends the current goroutine forever.
A goroutine in an endless for {} with no exit lives until process end.
What does runtime.Goexit do?
questions.answer: Ends the current goroutine after running defers. It is not a panic.

questions.text: Since Go 1.22, how does a for loop variable work when a goroutine captures it?
questions.answer: Each iteration has its own variable, not one for the whole loop.

questions.text: What does GOMAXPROCS limit?
questions.answer: How many threads run Go code at once, not how many goroutines exist.

questions.text: What is a data race between goroutines?
questions.answer: Concurrent memory access with no synchronization; the result is undefined.

questions.text: What does runtime.Gosched do?
questions.answer: Yields: the current goroutine may be taken off the thread.

questions.text: How does a goroutine stack grow?
questions.answer: From a small size, as needed; not a fixed OS-thread megabyte stack.

questions.text: Why is a forgotten goroutine in for {} a leak?
questions.answer: It never exits and holds resources until the process ends.

questions.text: Where does a local go if another goroutine reads its address?
questions.answer: It is moved to the heap; the pointer stays live.
